title: Smokescreen Saturday Exposed: Chris Packham Blasts The Quorn Hunt Over Sickening Fox Cruelty That Blows Apart Trail Hunting’s Biggest Lie
content:
When we showed wildlife campaigner Chris Packham the sickening footage of the Quorn Hunt, his response was damning:




“Another bloody year, another bloodied body, another animal tortured and torn to pieces to gratify the bloodlust of savages. Where is the damned consultation and where is the damned ban?”




Chris Packham condemns the Quorn Hunt footage.




The footage lays bare the brutal reality of cub hunting – the practice of using foxes to train young hounds to hunt and kill.




WARNING: DISTURBING FOOTAGE










Cub hunting is not some isolated activity. It is the preparation for the hunting season ahead. Throughout the autumn, young hounds are taught what to chase, what to kill and how to respond to the huntsman’s commands. What they learn – or fail to learn – during these crucial weeks sets the tone for the entire season.




This is what makes the Quorn Hunt footage so damning. It shows hounds being deliberately encouraged to seize and tear at a fox, with hunt staff repeatedly intervening to reinforce that behaviour.




On the eve of National Trail Hunting Day aka Smokescreen Saturday – as the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) and the Countryside Alliance prepared to showcase so-called ‘trail hunting’, the Quorn Hunt provided a horrifying glimpse of the reality behind the myth of trail laying.

title: All Warning, No Action?
content:
As more hunts receive police warnings and notices, are they a route to meaningful action, or a substitute for it?




Many of you cannot have failed to notice that we are writing more and more about hunts being issued with Community Protection Warnings (CPWs) and, occasionally, the CPW’s big sister, the Community Protection Notice (CPN). The former of course precedes the latter.




What in the puck is this? The Puckeridge and Essex Hunts have had 3 CPWs and a CPN and they still ignore them. Image: East Herts Hunt Sabs.




The Community Protection Notice system, including the requirement to issue a warning first, was introduced in 2014 by David Cameron’s Conservative-led coalition government, under then Home Secretary Theresa May as part of the Anti-social Behaviour, Crime & Policing Act 2014.




The irony that these measures are now being used, more and more, to regulate the conduct of fox hunts, an activity that has recently been publicly defended by Cameron, is not lost on us.




A CPW is not a criminal conviction. Ignoring one is not, in itself, a criminal offence, and there is no automatic penalty for failing to comply. If the behaviour continues, the police can escalate matters by issuing a CPN. Unlike a warning, a CPN imposes legally enforceable requirements, and breaching those requirements without reasonable excuse is a criminal offence.

title: The Law Catches up with the Lauderdale: Huntswoman Convicted of Illegal Fox Hunting
content:
Claire Bellamy, 51, veteran huntswoman for the Lauderdale Hunt, became the first fox hunter convicted under Scotland’s new hunting laws, following a case in which footage captured by Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs exposed illegal hunting taking place beyond the boundaries of licensed operation.




Claire Bellamy after the incident. Image: Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs




On Monday, 5 October 2026, Bellamy, the former master and huntsman was found guilty at Paisley Sheriff Court of deliberately hunting a fox with dogs during an outing at Kirkton Wood, between Houston and Kilmacolm in January, 2025.




The hunt had been granted a licence by NatureScot, allowing dogs to be used under controlled circumstances. But the footage, which was played to the court, showed the hounds pursuing a fox outside the area covered by that licence.




Under the Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023, NatureScot can licence more than two dogs to search for, stalk or flush a fox from cover, where this is necessary to prevent serious damage and where an alternative control is not available – it is not a licence to hunt foxes in any traditional sense.




This fox was hunted as hounds were allowed to hunt in the open. Image: Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs

title: The Rural Connections Behind Illegal Hunting
content:
Thanks to Wiltshire Hunt Sabs for this guest post, who, alongside Cirencester Illegal Hunt Watch, Bristol Hunt Sabs and Bath Hunt Sabs, have been keeping the pressure on the Beaufort Hunt.




The Duke of Beaufort’s Hunt is one of Britain’s most prominent fox hunts and has been terrorising wildlife across the countryside surrounding the Badminton Estate in Gloucestershire for hundreds of years. But the Beaufort Hunt does not exist in isolation. Behind it lies a wider rural network of landowners, estate managers and property professionals.




One of the most striking examples is Rupert Sturgis, Partner and Head of Knight Frank’s Cirencester office.




Rupert Sturgis, Partner and Head of Knight Frank, Cirencester. Image: Wiltshire Hunt Sabs




Knight Frank’s website describes Sturgis as specialising in the sale of town and country property across Gloucestershire and North Wiltshire.




Screenshot: 

Knight Frank




He is also a Field Master of the Beaufort Hunt.




On Saturday we filmed Rupert directing the field riders to surround a covert. This is so foxes become trapped inside, whilst hounds are sent in to kill them. It’s a classic cubbing technique that teaches the new hounds to kill.




Rupert Sturgis directing the field to surround the covert in a classic cubbing formation. Image: Wiltshire Hunt Sabs

title: Eggesford in the Dock: Huntsman Convicted of Illegal Hunting
content:
Eggesford Hunt huntsman Jason Marles has been convicted of illegally hunting a fox with hounds following an incident captured on drone footage during the hunt’s Boxing Day meet in December 2025.




Jason Marles, huntsman of the Eggesford Hunt.




Marles, 44, pleaded guilty to hunting a wild mammal with dogs at Pudson Farm, near Okehampton, when he appeared before Exeter Magistrates’ Court on 23 September 2026.




His conviction followed footage recorded by Devon County Hunt Saboteurs which showed a fox being bolted from an area of rubble before being pursued by hounds. Hunt saboteurs positioned on a farm track nearby were in position to stop the hounds from chasing the fox, and they confirmed that the fox managed to evade capture.




The footage shows Marles standing beside the area where the fox had taken refuge, close to a cattle barn. Two men with spades are moving rubble and digging at the site, while a child, who had dismounted from their pony, also watches what is happening.




Huntsman Jason Marles looks on as landowner Lloyd Heard and terrier-man Tom Bounsall dig and remove the rubble protecting the hunted fox. Image credit: Devon County Hunt Saboteurs.




Devon County Hunt Sabs identify the two men digging as Eggesford terrier man Tom Bounsall and landowner Lloyd Heard.
